coredata.dc:description: The quest for more sustainable structural epoxy resin (ER) adhesives is of major importance, environmentally and economically. A more friendly-environmental ER based on itaconic acid (IA), bisphenol A (BPA) and epichlorohydrin (ECH) was synthesized without the use of a catalyst. The obtained products were chemically characterized by means of 1H NMR and ATR-FTIR spectroscopy analysis. Thermal properties and rheological performances of the developed pre-polymer resins were also studied, and the final properties compared with a well-known commercial epoxy resin (ER-SIKA). Overall, the increase of IA content, resulted in a decrease of the glass transition temperature (Tg) of the pre-polymer resins, with values ranging between −9 °C and 31 °C. The obtained results showed that the prepared biobased ERs presented promising features for future crosslinking and can replace totally or partially BPA based ERs.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The quest for more sustainable structural epoxy resin (ER) adhesives is of major importance, environmentally and economically. A more friendly-environmental ER based on itaconic acid (IA), bisphenol A (BPA) and epichlorohydrin (ECH) was synthesized without the use of a catalyst. The obtained products were chemically characterized by means of 1H NMR and ATR-FTIR spectroscopy analysis. Thermal properties and rheological performances of the developed pre-polymer resins were also studied, and the final properties compared with a well-known commercial epoxy resin (ER-SIKA). Overall, the increase of IA content, resulted in a decrease of the glass transition temperature (Tg) of the pre-polymer resins, with values ranging between −9 °C and 31 °C. The obtained results showed that the prepared biobased ERs presented promising features for future crosslinking and can replace totally or partially BPA based ERs.

ce:section.ce:para: Epoxy resins (ERs) are widely used as structural adhesives, mainly due to their unique properties, such as, strong adhesion capacity to several substrates (metallic and non-metallic), excellent dielectric properties, low shrinkage, high hardness and good flexibility, among others [1]. These characteristics generates materials with high performances and with a broad range of possible applications, from civil engineering to aerospace fields [2,3]. Recently, a lot of attention is being given to these thermosetting resins based on renewable resources, mainly due to the increase of global pollution, which is evident by the increase of wastes disposals and therefore the increase of CO2 production. Paired with these environmental considerations, the possibility of having low production costs and possible biodegradable materials results in the replacement, partial or total, of bisphenol A (BPA) by more eco-friendly alternatives [4–7].

Vegetable oils such as soybean oil, linseed oil and castor oil, as well as their epoxidized forms [6,8,9]; polysaccharides, such as cellulose and starch; furan-based systems; tannins [10,11]; epoxidized natural rubber; lignin [12] and rosin-based resins [13,14], are some of the most common green alternatives to the typical diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A based resins (DGEBA). Among these DGEBA alternatives, itaconic acid (IA) is drawing a lot of attention as a potential starting material for the preparation of biobased ERs [15–18]. IA is produced by the fermentation of carbohydrate, e.g., glucose, in the presence of Aspergillus terreus. It is one of the top 12 potential biobased platform chemicals by the U.S. Department of Energy [19] corroborating its potential in replacing the BPA based resins [18]. The potential of this unsaturated dicarboxylic acid can be explained by the promising possibilities of the α,β-unsaturated double bond that enable several chemical modifications and therefore, increases the possibility of tailoring the final properties of the synthesized materials [20,21]. Recently, this building block has been widely explored in the development of new biobased polyesters [22–24] and can be crosslinked by thermal and UV methods. Its use in a wide range of fields is also well-known, from biomedical areas (drug release, hydrogels, elastomers [25–27]) to industrial ones (flame retardants [28], emulsion paints and coatings [29]), mainly due to their high modulus, strength, and glass transition temperature [21,30].

In this context, biobased ERs having different amounts of IA, ECH and BPA were synthesized and fully characterized. The chemical, thermal, and rheological properties were studied, and the results compared with a commercial DGEBA resin.

4,4′-isopropylidenediphenol or bisphenol A, BPA (97%), epichlorohydrin, ECH (99%), itaconic acid, IA (99%) and phenolphthalein were purchased from Acros Organics. Sodium hydroxide, NaOH (98%) was obtained from VWR Chemicals BDH®. Pyridine (99.5%) was purchased from Fischer Chemicals. Hydrochloric acid (37%) was purchased from Riedel-de Haën. A structural adhesive was kindly provided by SIKA (a two-part toughened epoxy resin system consisting of Part A (DGEBA) and a Part B (hardener). All chemicals were used as received.

For the preparation of ERs with different proportions of IA, first 0.1 mol of BPA were mixed with a solution of NaOH (0.188 mol) in a 250 mL four-necked flask, fitted with a thermometer, reflux condenser and equipped with a mechanical stirrer. The content of the flask was heated on an oil bath at 50 °C for 10 min; 0.16 mol of ECH were added in one bath, followed by the addition of IA in different proportions (0.02–0.08 mol). Temperature was raised to 95 °C within 20 min and held steady for 40 min. The temperature should not exceed 95 °C since high temperatures favor side reactions. The reflux condenser was removed, and the stirrer switched off so that the formed pre-polymer could settle down. The clear aqueous upper layer was carefully removed, and the product washed by vigorously stirring with distilled water at 80–95 °C. The material was left to settle, and the washing water was removed. The final resin was washed several times until a constant pH was attained.

The determination of the epoxy value was performed by pyridinium chloride method [31,32]. Thus, 0.1–0.2 g of the epoxy resin were mixed with 2 mL of HCl, in 25 mL of pyridine. The mixture was heated to reflux in a water bath for 45 min. The solution was cooled to room temperature and the un-reacted acid present in it was estimated by back titration with standard NaOH solution (0.1 N) using phenolphthalein indicator. A blank was also carried out under the same reaction conditions. Epoxide equivalent value of the resin can be calculated according to equation (1) and can be expressed as eq/Kg or as wpe (weight per equivalent, eq/g).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Attenuated total reflectance - fourier transform Infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR)
ce:section.ce:para: ATR-FTIR analyses of the ERs were carried out with a Jasco FT-IR-4200 spectrometer, from Jasco Inc. (Easton, USA) equipped with a Golden Gate Single Reflection Diamond ATR. Data collection was performed with 4 cm−1 spectral resolution and 128 accumulations.

The 1H NMR spectra of the commercial structural adhesive and of the synthesized new biobased ERs were obtained on a 9.4 T Spectrometer, at room-temperature and using (CHCl3) chloroform as solvent. Tetramethylsilane (TMS) was used as the internal reference.

A controlled stress rheometer, Haake, model RS1, was used to study the rheological behavior of the samples. The geometry used was a plate/plate system PP20 (titanium for the rotating part and stainless steel for the stationary part). The gap was set as 0.5 mm and the shear stress was defined between 0.5 and 250 Pa. The temperature of 25 °C was maintained constant during the rheological measurements of the itaconic-based ERs.

The thermal stability of the ERs was evaluated by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) in the range of ca. 25–600 °C, in a TA Instruments Q500 thermogravimetric analyzer (thermobalance sensitivity: 0.1 μg) at a heating rate of 10 °C·min−1 and under a dry nitrogen purge flow of 100 mL min−1.

The differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurements were performed in a Q100 DSC model (TA Instruments, USA), equipped with a RCS90 cooling unit. The polymers were analyzed in aluminum pans with a loosely placed ordinary aluminum lid. All scans were done in a dry nitrogen environment with a purge flow of 50 mL⋅min−1 and a heating rate of 5 °C⋅min−1 ranging from −80 to 150 °C.

Dynamic mechanical thermal analyses (DMTA) were performed in a Tritec 2000 DMA equipment and the polymers were analyzed in the single cantilever bending geometry. The tests were carried out from −150 °C to 200 °C, in a multifrequency mode (1 Hz and 10 Hz), with a standard heating rate of 5 °C min−1. The Tg was determined from the maximum of tan δ, at 1 Hz.

The synthesis of the itaconic-based ERs was performed via reaction between ECH, BPA and IA. The schematic representation of these synthesis is presented in Fig. 1 . The introduction of IA allows enhancing the bio-character of the final epoxy resin and create an extra site for curing reactions (the crosslinking sites are red marked in Fig. 1).

Concerning the structural adhesives application, more environmental-friendly materials with similar behavior to commercial petroleum-based ERS, containing different proportions of IA were synthesized. The composition of the ERs and respective epoxy values, determined by the pyridine/HCl method, can be seen in Table 1 . The large difference in epoxy value might be explained by the difference in the amount of ECH. The excess of epichlorohydrin might limit the branching reactions and thus minimize the reactions of phenolic hydroxyls with the epoxy groups present in the molecules [33]. Therefore, less epoxy groups are present by molecule. The pre-polymers denominated as ER4 and ER5 showed values of epoxy equivalent very similar to the one obtained for the commercial product ER-SIKA, using the same method under the same conditions. These values were expected for this type of materials and described in the literature [34,35].

ATR-FTIR and 1HNMR were used to chemically characterize the structural adhesives. The ATR-FTIR spectra of the developed ERs and of the commercial ER-SIKA pre-polymer are presented in Fig. 2 A and Fig. 2B, respectively. Some differences were detected between the two spectra. These differences are attributed to the distinct chemical structure of SIKA adhesive, a well-known DGEBA-based epoxy resin [36]. In Fig. 2A, the band assigned to the –OH stretching (a) is visible at 3400–3300 cm−1 for all the prepared polymers, while for the commercial product this band is almost imperceptible. At 2950 cm−1 and 2870 cm−1 (b) the asymmetric and symmetric C–H stretch of the methyl and methylene groups were observed. It is also possible to observe at 1720 cm−1 (c) the band assigned to the carbonyl (CO) stretch and at 1620 cm−1 (d) to the alkenyl (CC) stretch [15]. The incorporation of IA is confirmed by the presence of these bands. The aromatic rings of BPA are assigned at 1615 cm−1 and 1520 cm−1 (e) [37]. The ether bonds of the epoxide groups were detected at 1240 cm−1 for both the synthetized and the commercial pre-polymer [37,38]. Moreover, the band detected at 911 cm−1 for the prepared ERs and at 908 cm−1 for the ER-SIKA is characteristic of the oxirane rings (f) present in the pre-polymer structure.

Further insights onto the chemical structure of the partially biobased ERs were obtained by 1H NMR spectroscopy. The 1H NMR spectra of ER-SIKA and the synthesized itaconic-based ER1 and ER5, are shown in Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 , respectively. 1H NMR of all samples are similar and the ones of ER2, ER3 and ER4 are presented in SI (Fig. S1).

From Fig. 3 is possible to distinguish the resonance signals characteristics of the BPA moiety, at 7.1 ppm and 6.8 ppm (d), from the aromatic protons [39]. The peak at 1.6 ppm is ascribed to the methyl protons (e). The peaks observed at 2.9–2.7 ppm (a), 3.3 ppm (b) and at 4.2–3.9 ppm (c), correspond to the protons of the ethylene oxide ring. In Fig. 4, the spectra of the ER1 and ER5, besides the protons ascribed to the aromatic ring and to the ethylene oxide ring, were also detected the protons of the IA. Moreover, ER5, the resin with the high amount of IA, was detected the presence of the unsaturated protons from itaconic double bond at 6.3 ppm and 5.7 ppm (i) (highlighted in the spectrum) [15]. However, ER1, the resin with the lowest amount of IA (0.04 mol), these protons were not visible, possible due to a lower incorporation of IA. Still, for both ER1 and ER5, -O-CH
2 -(f, h) and –CH2-CH(OH)–CH2- (g) protons of IA were detected at 4.3 ppm and at 4.1 ppm, respectively. A multiplet at 3.6 ppm was also identified, –CC–CH
2 –CC- (j), in both spectra, which is assigned to IA [15]. The results are indicative of the reaction between IA and ECH.

The viscosity of an ER is one of the most important properties since it is a key factor to determine the final application of a thermosetting resin. However, considering that these types of materials are composed by two distinct parts, a pre-polymer and a hardener, it is possible to tailor the final viscosity of the ER by changing the type and amount of pre-polymer and/or hardener added to the formulation. The rheological behavior of the synthesized epoxy materials, at a variable shear stress was analyzed and the obtained results are presented in Fig. 5 .

The viscosity of formulations ER1 and ER2 were impossible to measure, since high variations during the assay were obtained, mostly due to the brittle nature of the samples. Therefore only the pre-polymers ER3 to ER5 are herein presented and discussed. According to Fig. 5, the viscosity of ER4 (η = 1000 Pa s) is much lower than the viscosity obtained for ER3 (η = 4259 Pa s) and for ER5 (η = 6500 Pa s). This result is directly related with the amount of IA and ECH present in the formulations, meaning that a higher amount of IA added to the formulation resulted in a lower viscosity of the epoxy materials [40] which is corroborated also by the ER5 and ER4 formulations results. On the other hand, increasing the ECH content, a result in the decrease of the viscosity as can be perceived by the results of ER3 and ER4. Therefore, higher amounts of ECH and IA resulted in a significant decrease of viscosity. Also, at room temperature, the viscosity was linear, with no significant variations with the increase of shear rate. The viscosity of ER-SIKA was also determined and compared with the described in the product data sheet (η = 430 Pa s, at 20 °C and 10 sec−1). Under the conditions previously described, ER-SIKA showed a similar behavior, with a viscosity of 600 Pa s, which was a little higher than expected. The differences detected between the obtained viscosity with theoretical one, as well as the high values observed for the remaining samples, is probably related with the fact that all the samples were previously dried, which ultimately resulted in an enhancement of the final viscosity of the tested materials.

The thermal stability of the synthesized pre-polymers was assessed by TGA and the obtained TGA curves and 1st derivative of TGA curves (DTG) curves are displayed in Fig. 6 . The degradation temperatures were determined considering the maximum peaks of the derivative curves and the results are displayed in Table 2 , such as 5% weight loss (T5%), 10% weight loss (T10%), and the residual weight percentage at 600 °C (R600). According with Fig. 6, the degradation of the commercial ER-SIKA resin occurs in two distinct steps [41], at 296 °C and at 405 °C, beginning to lose weight at 220 °C and degrading almost completely at 600 °C. However, the synthesized epoxy materials revealed a three-stage thermal degradation, with the first step occurring around 100 °C. Although all the pre-polymers were dried before thermal characterization analysis, the presence of residual water was detected, and can be assigned to this first decomposition stage.

The second and third degradation steps are very similar for the prepared pre-polymers and match the degradation stages of the commercial ER. The degradation stage occurring around 290–340 °C can be attributed to the degradation of the DGEBA, which occurs close to 300 °C [36]. The itaconic-based ERs showed similar degradation temperatures, ranging from 285 °C to 337 °C. The high thermal stability of these materials is in part due to the aromatic ring of BPA, present in all formulations. The second stage detected at 400 °C can be correlated to the complete degradation of smaller fragments of byproducts obtained during the synthesis of the resins. Moreover, it is possible to stablish a correlation between the thermal stability and the amount of IA incorporated into the ERs. According to Fig. 6, ER1 and ER2 have very similar thermal profiles. Although the weight loss at 5% is higher for ER2, this prepolymer as a Td very similar to ER1. ER2 has a slightly higher thermal stability than ER1, which can be related with the higher amount of IA incorporate. Regarding ER2 and ER3 thermal stabilities, the increase on the amount of IA resulted in a small decrease of Td from 424.5 °C to 395.6 °C, although T5% and T10% were higher for ER3. The results on Table 2 and Fig. 6 suggests that the presence of IA in the ERs structure led to materials with a slight loss of thermal stability. This phenomenon could be explained by the presence of ester linkages, which are easily cleaved [15]. Also, this can be related with the decrease of R600 with the increase of the IA amount on ERs structure.

When the amount of ECH was increased, a higher Td was noticed (for the 2nd and the 3rd stage) – ER4 showed higher stability than ER3. The increase on the content of IA resulted in a decrease of the thermal stability of the ER. The combination between the amount of ECH and IA in the pre-polymer ER5, resulted in a higher Td then the observed for ER-SIKA.

The Tg of the partially based-itaconic ERs was determined by DSC analysis and the results are shown in Table 3 and in SI (Fig. S2). The DSC heating curves of the pre-polymers exhibited similar behaviors, with Tg values ranging from −24 to 31 °C (see Table 3). Also, itaconic based ERs, ER1 and ER2, showed similar profile traces, with higher Tg results, which can be related to the higher amount of epoxy groups present in ER structure. The synthesized ER3, ER4 and ER5 presented Tg values between 3 and -9 °C. The commercial product exhibits a low Tg compared with the previous formulations, of −23.6 °C. The obtained Tg from the DSC heating curves were compared with the Tg values acquired from DMTA analysis.

In Fig. 7 , tan δ curves as a function of temperature of the itaconic-based ERs and ER-SIKA are displayed, where the materials were submitted to the frequencies of 1 and 10 Hz. DMTA allows to distinguish between frequency dependent and nondependent thermal events and molecular relaxations such as α (or glass transitions) are always frequency dependent. This technique also provides information about the morphology and miscibility of polymers – it is possible to evaluate the behavior of the polymer by the shifts in loss tangent peak temperature [41]. The maximum tan δ obtained for the studied resins is resumed in Table 3. The loss modulus (E’) and tan δ at 1 Hz and 10 Hz for each ERs is presented in Fig. S3, in SI. The Tg of ER-SIKA is characterized by a single narrow peak of tan δ at −15.4 °C. The theoretical Tg of commercial resin is of 67 °C, but this value corresponds to the cured epoxy material, thus a crosslinked matrix which obviously results in a polymer network with lower chain mobility. Most of the works developed until know are focused on the cured ERs, either with or without addition of biobased polymers or biobased hardeners.

However, it is crucial to understand the pre-polymer thermomechanical behavior before the curing process. It is possible to tune the Tg of the final epoxy cured resins by the right choice of type and amount of curing agent to be used, but also by the pre-polymer used. Even if it presents a high Tg, by adding a proper hardener or a mixture of hardeners and/or fillers, it is possible to adjust the final material properties to the desired application.

Concerning Table 3, Tg values obtained by DSC are in good agreement with Tg values obtained by DTMA analysis, with slight variations that can be easily explained by the differences in the principles used by each technique to determine the Tg. ER3 and ER4 pre-polymers showed to be the formulations with the highest tan δ, of 0.32 and 0.33, respectively and therefore the resins with the highest capacity to dissipate energy. The damping behavior is an important parameter considering the application of ERs in civil, automobile and aerospace, where the ability to dissipate noise and mechanical vibrations into heat is crucial. The higher tan δ, more effective is the material to dissipate the energy into heat [42].

The formulations ER4 and ER5 and commercial product presented a negative T g values, in contrast with the positive Tg values for the formulations ER1 to ER3. The increase in the amount of IA and ECH resulted in materials with more chain mobility than the previous formulations. The values of Tg are also in agreement with the equivalent epoxy values obtained by the pyridinium chloride method. A higher amount of epoxy groups leads also to less flexible materials with high Tg [40].

In this study, the synthesis of partially biobased ERs, based on IA, BPA and ECH, was performed and the resulting pre-polymer resins were extensively characterized. It was clear that the amount of IA added to the formulations of the pre-polymers determined the properties of the materials. The chemical reactions were confirmed by ATR-FTIR and 1HNMR analyses. Viscosity tends to decrease with the increase of IA and with the increase of ECH content. Also, this renewable source will produce a final material with a higher crosslinking density due to their pendant vinylic group. Although the increase of IA resulted in a slight decrease of ERs thermal stability, the obtained Td are very similar to the commercial product, characterized by a superior thermal stability. DSC and DMTA analysis showed Tg between −23 and 30 °C, where a higher amount of IA and ECH resulted in lower Tg, i.e. more flexible pre-polymers. The developed materials revealed to be suitable candidates to be further subject to crosslinking reactions and ultimately to be applied in industrial fields.
